extracted.intended_audience: journalists, science journalists, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for monitoring, reporting on, and handling retracted scientific papers — aimed at journalists and journal editors who cover or manage corrections and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of concern (definition and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'expression of concern' is 'A statement issued by the editor of a peer-reviewed journal … [that] calls attention to a specific paper, especially to question the validity of that paper or portions of that paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an expression of concern to publicly flag potential validity problems in a paper when issues are identified but a full retraction or correction is not yet appropriate; it is a formal editorial notice to draw attention to specific concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for inconsistency in how retractions are handled
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the messages we hope make clear is that a lot of what we're looking for is inconsistency. 'Do you always do the same thing [with retractions] based on the last time you did it? That’s one of the major things I look for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journals and publishers by whether they apply consistent procedures across similar cases; inconsistency is a red flag and a valid beat for watchdog reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction and downstream recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Although retractions are on average occurring sooner after publication than in the past, citation analysis shows that they are not being recognised by subsequent users of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both how quickly problematic papers are retracted or flagged and whether later users/citations notice those retractions; timeliness must include mechanisms to alert the research community so invalid work is not propagated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and clarity of reasons in retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons published in the retraction notice are not always reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices should state clear, reliable reasons for the retraction; vague or misleading notices reduce trust and hinder understanding. Journalism should scrutinize the stated reasons and, where necessary, seek clarifying evidence or explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive notification mechanisms for affected readers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not as much linkage as there could be. 'I’m not sure they do have a decent mechanism for alerting people who downloaded the original paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and advocate for technical solutions (trackbacks, citation linkage, and direct alerts to people who downloaded papers) so that readers and researchers who used the original paper are notified of retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and prominence of retractions/corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions, like their counterparts in magazines, newspapers, and online, often slip by unnoticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure corrections and retractions are made prominent (not buried), across all platforms where the original content appeared, to avoid continued dissemination of false or flawed findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness and transparency by journal editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafer didn’t stick his head in the sand ... He notified his readers of the retractions, revamped his journal’s author guidelines, and has been willing to talk about the case from the first moment. 'Openness should be the default, not the exception.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate editorial responses on transparency: timely public acknowledgment, clear communication with readers, willingness to discuss the case, and visible corrective action are best practices. Reticence to engage is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy revision and proactive corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: He notified his readers of the retractions, revamped his journal’s author guidelines, and has been willing to talk about the case from the first moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond issuing retractions, journals should revise policies and author guidelines to prevent recurrence; effective handling includes both remediation (retraction/correction) and systemic policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of independent watchdogs and specialized reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction Watch ... should be required reading for anyone interested in scientific journalism or the issue of accuracy. The pair hope to bring awareness to the retractions ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent blogs and watchdogs that track retractions provide accountability and public service; evaluate such outlets by their expertise, track record (e.g., previous fraud exposes), and ability to surface both recent and historical problematic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate technical retraction notices into accessible explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: They will provide an invaluable service by offering layman’s translations of retractions such as this: [example retraction text].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice for journalists and watchdogs is to interpret and explain retraction notices in plain language so non-specialist readers can understand the implications; this improves accountability and public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections should acknowledge errors, apologise, and remedy harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction example: 'We now accept that there was no truth in these allegations and we and other media have agreed to pay him damages and have apologised to Mr Subramanyam for the distress and embarrassment caused.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective corrections should explicitly acknowledge the error, apologise when appropriate, and, where relevant, note remediation (e.g., damages, apologies). This level of candor is a standard for ethical journalism and publishing.
